judgments.title: SYARIKAT AIR MELAKA BERHAD v FASIHAH BINTI ZAMRAN & ors
judgments.catchwords: TORT — Negligence — Road obstruction — Motorcyclist colliding with unlit signboard on dark bend — Ownership and responsibility inferred from utility’s label and absence of explanation — Child pillion’s direct evidence supported by physical and contemporaneous evidence — Photographs of disturbed scene not establishing original position of board — Suggested pothole cause remaining speculative — Duty to place, maintain and remove signboard safely breached — Liability upheld. TORT — Contributory negligence — Burden on defendant — Pillion’s sighting of obstruction not establishing rider’s opportunity to avoid it — No evidence of speed, visibility distance, reaction time, braking distance or room to swerve — Inference of want of care based on hindsight — Helmet allegation unsupported — Finding of 10% contributory negligence set aside — Defendant wholly liable — Civil Law Act 1956, s 12(1). DAMAGES — Personal injuries — Severe traumatic brain injury — Permanent total dependency — Bedridden patient retaining awareness distinguished from persistent vegetative state — Global award covering neurological sequelae — RM400,000 within applicable Compendium range — Less disabling injuries unsuitable comparators — No basis for appellate reduction. DAMAGES — Special damages — Family’s travelling expenses during hospitalisation — Daily visits and reasonable journey cost established by uncontradicted oral evidence — Absence of receipts not fatal — Strict proof assessed according to nature of expenditure and available evidence — Award of RM2,200 upheld. DAMAGES — Loss of future earnings — Cash-paid worker at family food stall — Related witnesses’ evidence requiring assessment rather than rejection merely for relationship — Employment corroborated by medical histories and unchallenged testimony — Absence of wage records or statutory contributions not defeating claim — Statutory sixteen-year multiplier applied without further contingency deduction — RM215,040 awarded — Civil Law Act 1956, s 28A(2). DAMAGES — Future care — Full-time helper required on both parties’ expert evidence — Gratuitous care by mother not relieving tortfeasor of liability — Discretionary welfare payment not deductible — Recurring recruitment costs assessed over successive two-year contracts — Award reassessed at RM819,472. DAMAGES — Future medical expenses — Competing expert costings — Later assessment reflecting stabilised condition preferred — Supplier’s quotation proving price rather than required quantity — Nutrition, consumables and replacement equipment distinguished from free public hospital treatment — Possibility of government assistance not proof of assured provision — RM356,970 awarded. DAMAGES — Future care and medical expenses — Deduction for contingencies and accelerated receipt — Non-statutory multipliers distinguished from statutory earnings multiplier — Injury-specific survival tables already accounting for reduced life expectancy — Further mortality discount constituting double deduction — Accelerated receipt considered alongside absence of allowance for rising costs — Unreasoned one-third deductions set aside. CIVIL PROCEDURE — Appeal — Findings based on inference and assessment of expert evidence — Unsupported contributory negligence finding and rejection of earnings evidence on relationship alone — Unexplained choice of care costings — Appellate reassessment without remittal — Utility’s appeal dismissed and plaintiffs’ appeal allowed — Total damages varied to RM1,818,202.
judgments.judge: YA Dato' Sri Raja Segaran A/L S.Krishnan

judgments.title: PLENTIFIELD MARKETING SDN. BHD. v TENAGA NASIONAL BERHAD
judgments.catchwords: CIVIL PROCEDURE — Interlocutory injunction — Electricity supply to operating hotel — Threatened disconnection for substantial arrears pending judicial management application — Serious issues concerning statutory notice, amount payable and interaction of statutory regimes — Preservation of existing supply — Injunction granted subject to payment and security conditions — Courts of Judicature Act 1964, s 25 and Schedule, para 6 — Rules of Court 2012, O 29 r 1. COMPANY LAW — Judicial management — Moratorium upon filing application — Meaning of “other legal process” — Regulatory disconnection distinguished from court process and expressly prohibited distress — Provisional construction that moratorium does not itself prohibit disconnection notice or discontinuance of supply — General injunctive jurisdiction remaining available — Rescue purpose relevant to exercise of discretion — Companies Act 2016, s 410(c). COMPANY LAW — Judicial management — Essential supplies — Interval before judicial management order — Statutory protection against insistence on pre-order arrears applying only after order — Protection not automatically extended to applicant awaiting determination — Policy informing interlocutory discretion without displacing statutory conditions — Continued supply secured by payment for new consumption and existing deposit — Companies Act 2016, s 414(7). ELECTRICITY — Disconnection for non-payment — Compliance with amended notice requirements — Identification of defaulting bill and date of presentation — Thirty-day payment period, fourteen-day notice window and seven working days before disconnection — Meaning of six-month provision — Service on corporate consumer and effect of actual receipt — Serious issues reserved for final determination — Licensee Supply Regulations 1990, regs 4(1)(b), 4(2) and 4(2A), as amended in 2025. CIVIL PROCEDURE — Injunction — Bona fide dispute over electricity charges — Payments omitted from sum claimed in recovery action — Surcharge included as current bill — Possible overlap between surcharge and interest — Inconsistent metering and aging records — Dispute arising from supplier’s own documents rather than bare denial — No final determination of indebtedness. judgments.title: CHUNG CHEE YANG v Pendakwa Raya
judgments.catchwords: Criminal appeals - against the whole of the decision of the Magistrate’s Court Amendment of charges - s. 158(1) of the CPC grants the court broad discretion to alter or add to a charge at any point during a trial prior to the delivery of judgment - the optimal window to amend or introduce a charge is at the conclusion of the prosecution's case, provided that such an amendment does not cause irremediable prejudice to the substantive rights of the accused person Recall of witnesses following the amendment of a charge - the court's obligation to grant an opportunity to recall or re-summon past witnesses is triggered only upon a party's request, rather than operating as an automatic consequence of the amended charge - the trial court was under no legal duty to advise him of his rights under s. 162 of the CPC - the court is not under a duty to advise or prompt an accused person who is already fully and professionally represented by legal counsel on tactical choices or the exercise of procedural rights Presiding Magistrate recorded the guilty plea of the co-accused, before proceeding with the Appellant's trial - a presiding judge who records a co-accused's plea of guilt is not disqualified from continuing to try a remaining accused who has claimed his right to a full trial Criminal intimidation - essential ingredients of the offence comprise two prongs: first, the communication of a threat of injury to the victim's person, reputation, or property; and second, a distinct intent to cause alarm to that person - a threat need not be communicated through words alone; it may be manifested by conduct or any other threatening means - the omission of these verbal threats in the charge does not negate their existence or criminal intimidation The Prosecution’s failure to call the chief bodyguard - a settled principle that the Prosecution is under no legal obligation to call every available witness to narrate the same chain of events, provided there is no suppression or withholding of evidence Intention to shoot - a well-entrenched principle of criminal law that intention, being a subjective state of mind, may be proved through irresistible inferences drawn from the surrounding circumstances and is rarely capable of direct proof First information report - the primary purpose of a police report is to set the machinery of criminal investigation into motion. It is not required to contain every exhaustive fact. Instead, it suffices if the report enables the police to initiate an investigation. Defence as an afterthought - in criminal jurisprudence, the defence must present its case at the earliest possible stage. A failure to cross-examine on a core line of defence entitles the trial court to characterize it as a fabricated afterthought Custodial sentences - a sentencing court must be guided by the "one transaction rule" and the "totality principle".
